Switchover

Re-integration

Quick visual
Roles: Primary → Standby

When to switchover
Maintenance, upgrades, or testing — zero data loss when performed correctly.

screens.title: Failover vs Switchover
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two role-change events precisely. A failover is an unplanned promotion of a standby because the primary has become unavailable due to a crash, network outage, or critical software error. The objective in a failover is speed: restore write availability quickly, but you may face an unknown final state from the failed primary. That unknown state is why asynchronous replication can lead to data loss during failover. A switchover is the opposite: it's a planned and controlled role swap. Before a switchover you stop writes on the primary, wait for standbys to replay outstanding WAL so they are fully caught up, and then promote a chosen standby. That sequence guarantees zero data loss. A common misconception is that both actions are interchangeable; they are not. A switchover gives you an opportunity to ensure all replicas match the primary's state. In contrast, a failover requires acceptance of operational constraints and careful checks to avoid promoting an outdated replica. Consider a maintenance window: choose switchover for zero-loss updates. In an emergency, accept failover with the safety checks you'll learn next. Which approach you choose will determine the post-promotion steps for re-integrating the old primary.

keyIdea.title: Definition focus
keyIdea.text: Failover = emergency promotion with risk; Switchover = planned swap with zero-loss when properly executed.

content.html:
Definition
Failover vs Switchover
Clear operational differences determine risk and required checks.
Failover (Unplanned)
Triggered by an unexpected primary outage. Goal is fast promotion; data loss possible if standbys lag.
Switchover (Planned)
Planned maintenance or testing. Stop writes, let standbys catch up, and promote to ensure zero data loss.
Common misconception
Treating failovers like switchovers risks data loss. Failovers need extra fencing and validation.
Why it matters
Choosing the right procedure preserves consistency and reduces recovery time.
Analogy
Think of a switchover as an orderly handoff during shift change: you finish work, hand over all paperwork, and the next person continues without loss. A failover is an emergency evacuation: you focus on saving lives and may lose some records along the way.
Quick checklist
  • Is the standby's replay_lsn current?
  • Has the old primary been fenced or confirmed down?
  • Are application connections ready to point to the new primary?
Key Takeaway

Use switchover for planned zero-loss operations. Reserve failover for emergencies and apply fencing and LSN checks before promoting.

screens.title: Manual Failover Step-by-Step
screens.narratorSegment: When the primary fails, a disciplined process reduces mistakes. Start by identifying which standby is most up-to-date: run the LSN checks on each standby to compare pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn. The standby with the highest replay_lsn is your safest candidate. Next, promote the chosen standby using pg_ctl promote; this stops recovery and enables writes. Avoid ad-hoc removal of standby. signal unless you understand the consequences; pg_ctl promote is the recommended path. After promotion, the critical operational step is updating application connection strings, DNS records, or load balancer targets to point to the new primary. Without this, clients continue to try the failed host and your system stays unavailable. Then, handle the remaining standbys: they will still be configured to replicate from the old primary and will stop receiving WAL. Common options are to rebuild them with a fresh base backup from the new primary or attempt pg_rewind if timelines permit. Lastly, treat the old primary as a node to be re-integrated later; do not allow it to come back online accepting writes. This structured flow keeps recovery fast and safe. What step would you automate first in your environment?

keyIdea.title: Failover flow
keyIdea.text: Identify freshest standby, promote, update connections, rebuild or rewind other standbys, then re-integrate the old primary safely.

content.html:
Process Flow
Manual Failover Steps
  1. Choose a standby: verify pg_last_wal_replay_lsn on each standby to find the most current node.
  2. Promote the standby: run pg_ctl promote to stop recovery and accept writes.
  3. Update connections: change DNS, load balancer, or app config to the new primary's address.
  4. Handle other standbys: either rebuild from pg_basebackup or use pg_rewind if safe.
  5. Re-integrate old primary: wait to bring it back as a standby after a base backup or rewind.
Key Takeaway

Follow a strict sequence: pick the freshest standby, promote, redirect clients, and then reconcile the remaining servers to avoid split-brain.

Concrete example
-- On each standby, check LSNs
SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();

-- On the chosen standby, promote
sudo pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/main_standby promote

-- After promotion, verify not in recovery
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
Common mistake
Promoting an outdated standby without checking replay_lsn causes data loss.
Pro tip
Automate LSN collection across standbys so you can quickly compare replay positions under pressure.

screens.title: Inspecting LSN: pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct standby hinges on understanding WAL positions. Two standard standby-side functions are pg_last_wal_receive_lsn, which reports the last WAL byte the standby has received from the primary, and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn, which shows the last WAL byte the standby has actually replayed into its data files. For failover safety, prioritize the highest replay_lsn because it reflects applied data. A common pitfall is to compare receive_lsn only: a standby may have received WAL but not yet replayed it, which still risks losing un-applied transactions after promotion. In practice you connect to each standby and run the S Q L checks provided in the chapter. After promotion, confirm the new primary is not in recovery. Also inspect pg_stat_replication on the new primary to learn the state of other standbys. Remember that time and network delays can create small differences; plan for a tolerance window and prefer synchronous standbys where zero-loss is required. Now we'll show exact commands you can copy into a lab environment for verification and practice. Inspecting LSN: pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn means compare replay_lsn across standbys and prefer the one with the highest applied wal to minimize data loss on promotion.. In practical terms, how to determine which standby is the freshest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: LSN verification
keyIdea.text: Compare replay_lsn across standbys and prefer the one with the highest applied WAL to minimize data loss on promotion.

content.html:
Commands
LSN checks on a standby
-- On each standby, run
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();"

-- On the old primary (if available), inspect replication
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT client_addr, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn FROM pg_stat_replication;"
Interpretation
Pick the standby with the highest replay_lsn. If two are equal, prefer the one with the fastest connectivity and lowest lag.
Explanation and example
If standby A shows a replay_lsn that matches the last sent_lsn recorded on the primary, it has applied all sent WAL. Standby B may have received more WAL but not applied it yet; promoting B risks losing un-applied transactions. When in doubt, wait if possible, or promote the more current node and accept the operational tradeoffs.
Misconception check
Received WAL equals safe to promote. Not always — check replay_lsn to be sure the data is applied.
Key Takeaway
Always compare replay_lsn across standbys; this gives you the most reliable signal of applied data.

keyIdea.title: Promotion commands
keyIdea.text: Use pg_ctl promote for safe, explicit promotion; trigger files and standby.signal removal are alternatives that require precise configuration knowledge.

content.html:
Promotion
pg_ctl promote
# On the chosen standby
sudo pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/main_standby promote

-- Verify role
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"  -- should return 'f' after promotion
Alternative: trigger file
If configured with recovery_target_action, creating the trigger file will promote. Use only when intentionally set up.
Caution
Confirm the old primary is fenced off before promotion to avoid split-brain.
Example verification
After promotion you can create a table to confirm write capability, and inspect pg_stat_replication on the new primary to see connected standbys.
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE TABLE new_primary_test (id INT);"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT client_addr, state, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;"
Pro tip
Perform a quick write test and keep application traffic paused until connection strings are updated to prevent split-brain scenarios.

screens.title: Updating Application Connections
screens.narratorSegment: After promoting a standby, your database cluster has a new address or role. The absolute critical next step is updating your application's connection string, DNS, or load balancer so client traffic reaches the new primary. Neglecting this leaves applications pointing at the failed host, producing downtime even though the database is now writable. Common mechanisms include updating DNS entry TTLs, changing a load balancer target, or altering application configuration. Each method has tradeoffs: DNS propagation delays can extend downtime unless TTLs were pre-configured low; load balancer updates are faster but require orchestration. A frequent mistake is to rely on automatic client retries without changing endpoints — clients retrying the down host do not magically discover the new primary. When testing, simulate connection switch by updating a single service to the new host and confirm transactions succeed. Also ensure health checks and monitoring pick up the new primary and that automated failover orchestrators, if used, are aware of the new topology. In short, promotion gives you a writable server; updating connections makes it useful. Updating Application Connections means promotion is incomplete until clients can reach the new primary; update dns, load balancers, or application configs immediately to restore service.. In practical terms, why this is the single most critical post-promotion step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Promotion is incomplete until clients can reach the new primary; update DNS, load balancers, or application configs immediately to restore service.

content.html:
Critical Step
Update Application Connection Targets
Failure to re-point clients causes continued downtime even after successful promotion.
Options
  • Change load balancer target to new primary address.
  • Update DNS records with low TTL in advance.
  • Reconfigure application connection strings directly if needed.
Tradeoffs
DNS propagation can be slow; load balancers are faster but require pre-planned health checks and automation.
Consequence
Neglecting an update results in continued service outage despite a functioning primary.
Scenario
If load balancer health checks are configured, you can flip traffic quickly. For DNS, plan TTLs ahead of maintenance so clients refresh records promptly.
# Example: verify connectivity to new primary
psql -h new_primary_ip -U app_user -c "SELECT 1;"

# If successful, proceed to switch application config or load balancer target
Check your monitoring
Ensure alerts and dashboards point at the new primary so future incidents are visible.

screens.title: Handling Other Standbys After Promotion
screens.narratorSegment: After promoting one standby, other replicas are left pointing at the old primary and will stop receiving WAL. You have two primary courses of action. The simplest and most bulletproof method is to stop each standby, clear its data directory, and perform a fresh pg_basebackup from the newly promoted primary. This guarantees consistent on-disk state and a clean timeline. The alternative is to use pg_rewind to synchronize a previously primary server back to the new primary, but pg_rewind only works when timelines have not diverged significantly and requires careful use. A mistaken use of pg_rewind on a diverged timeline can leave a node inconsistent. If you opt to rebuild, automate the base backup step to reduce human error and ensure permissions and replication slots are set correctly on the new primary. Finally, always verify the reconfigured standbys are streaming and replaying WAL by checking pg_stat_replication on the new primary. This step prevents surprises when the cluster is under load again. Handling Other Standbys After Promotion means either rebuild standbys from a fresh base backup or apply pg_rewind when safe; always verify streaming and replay status afterward.. In practical terms, reconfigure, rebuild, or rewind remaining replicas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Re-integrating the Old Primary
screens.narratorSegment: When the failed primary is recoverable, treat it as a node that must be rebuilt to avoid timeline conflicts. The safe, commonly recommended approach is to clear its data directory and take a fresh pg_basebackup from the current primary, using replication credentials and the -R option to create a standby configuration. The chapter also describes pg_rewind as an alternative: it can synchronize a former primary to the new primary if timelines have not diverged too much. But pg_rewind requires that the old primary's data files are available and that you carefully check the recovery timeline. Never simply restart the old primary and let it accept writes — doing so risks split-brain. After re-integrating, verify the restored server reports pg_is_in_recovery() true and that the new primary's pg_stat_replication shows it as a standby. This sequence preserves the cluster's integrity and restores redundancy. In operational practice, prefer scripted, repeatable steps for re-integration to minimize configuration drift and human error. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter lists several common pitfalls that teams repeatedly encounter. The most dangerous is split-brain: if the old primary unexpectedly comes back online and accepts writes while a standby has been promoted, you'll have two divergent transaction histories that can cause irreparable corruption. Prevent this by fencing the old host — keep it off the network or shut it down until re-integration. Promoting an outdated standby is another error: always check replay_lsn. Failing to update application connections is operationally fatal; the database may be restored but applications still point to the failed host. Misuse of pg_rewind is a subtler hazard: pg_rewind can reconcile histories only when timelines are compatible. For heavily diverged timelines, pg_rewind will not work and you must rebuild with a base backup. The safety lesson is simple: favor conservative, verifiable actions over shortcuts during incident response. Regular rehearsals in staging will reveal these pitfalls before they occur in production. keyIdea.text: Simulate primary stop, promote standby, update connections, rebuild old primary with pg_basebackup, and verify replication.

content.html:
Part 1 — Simulate and Promote
# On primary: simulate crash
sudo systemctl stop postgresql
echo "Primary server is now down." 

# On standby: check LSNs
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();"

# Promote standby
sudo pg_ctl -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/main_standby promote
Part 2 — Verify and Re-integrate
# Verify new primary
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"  -- expect 'f'
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE TABLE new_primary_test (id INT);"

# On old primary: prepare for re-integration
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/postgresql/12/main/*
sudo -u postgres pg_basebackup -h  -D /var/lib/postgresql/12/main -U replicator_user -P -v -R -W
sudo systemctl start postgresql

# Confirm standby
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"  -- expect 't'
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT * FROM new_primary_test;"
Safety First
During the lab keep the old primary offline until re-integration is complete to avoid split-brain. Time each step and capture logs for review.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's close by restating the most important concepts. First, failover is an emergency promotion and may risk data loss if standbys lag. Second, switchover is a planned role swap that can achieve zero data loss when you stop writes and wait for standbys to catch up. Third, pg_ctl promote is the recommended command to turn a standby into a primary; alternatives like trigger files require precise configuration. Fourth, split-brain happens when two servers accept writes simultaneously and must be prevented by fencing the old primary. Fifth, check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn when choosing a standby — that value shows applied WAL and is the safest signal. Sixth, pg_rewind can re-sync a recovered primary when timelines are compatible, but default to a fresh pg_basebackup if unsure. Keep these concepts in mind as operational rules when designing and rehearsing your availability strategy.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical understanding of how PostgreSQL handles role changes when the primary must be replaced. You'll learn the difference between a failover, which is an unplanned promotion of a standby when the primary has failed, and a switchover, which is a planned, controlled role swap. We'll focus on the manual steps you need to execute in PostgreSQL 12: how to choose the best standby by inspecting LSN values, how to promote a standby safely, how to update application connections, and how to bring the old primary back as a standby using a base backup or pg_rewind when appropriate. You will also see the common risks to avoid, such as split-brain and promoting an outdated standby, and why routine rehearsals and a clear communications plan are essential. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to perform a deliberate failover or switchover with awareness of the consequences and the checks that prevent data loss. Think of this chapter as the operational checklist you run through when availability matters most.

Across the next screens you'll master practical skills for keeping a PostgreSQL cluster available during maintenance and outages. First, you will be able to distinguish failover from switchover and explain the operational differences and risks for each. Second, you will perform a manual failover: choosing the most current standby using LSN checks and promoting it to primary. Third, you will learn how to re-integrate a failed primary or prepare a new standby using pg_basebackup or pg_rewind, and why timelines matter. Finally, you will identify common pitfalls such as split-brain and promoting an outdated standby, and learn safety checks that prevent them. Each objective pairs a measurable action with the reason it matters in production, so you can test and verify competence in a staging environment before operating on live systems.

This second objectives slide focuses on the measurable checks and tools you will use when performing role changes. You will learn to verify replication progress using pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn so you can choose the most current standby. You will practice using pg_ctl promote safely and learn the alternatives such as a configured trigger file or removing standby. signal when appropriate. You will learn the scenarios where pg_rewind can reconcile a recovered old primary and when a fresh pg_basebackup is the safer option. Finally, you will understand why rehearsing failovers and switchovers in staging is non-negotiable: real environments expose network, permission, and timing issues that a checklist catches. Each objective pairs a command or tool with a clear outcome you can verify, so you can demonstrate competence in a lab exercise.

Let's define the two role-change events precisely. A failover is an unplanned promotion of a standby because the primary has become unavailable due to a crash, network outage, or critical software error. The objective in a failover is speed: restore write availability quickly, but you may face an unknown final state from the failed primary. That unknown state is why asynchronous replication can lead to data loss during failover. A switchover is the opposite: it's a planned and controlled role swap. Before a switchover you stop writes on the primary, wait for standbys to replay outstanding WAL so they are fully caught up, and then promote a chosen standby. That sequence guarantees zero data loss. A common misconception is that both actions are interchangeable; they are not. A switchover gives you an opportunity to ensure all replicas match the primary's state. In contrast, a failover requires acceptance of operational constraints and careful checks to avoid promoting an outdated replica. Consider a maintenance window: choose switchover for zero-loss updates. In an emergency, accept failover with the safety checks you'll learn next. Which approach you choose will determine the post-promotion steps for re-integrating the old primary.

When the primary fails, a disciplined process reduces mistakes. Start by identifying which standby is most up-to-date: run the LSN checks on each standby to compare pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn. The standby with the highest replay_lsn is your safest candidate. Next, promote the chosen standby using pg_ctl promote; this stops recovery and enables writes. Avoid ad-hoc removal of standby. signal unless you understand the consequences; pg_ctl promote is the recommended path. After promotion, the critical operational step is updating application connection strings, DNS records, or load balancer targets to point to the new primary. Without this, clients continue to try the failed host and your system stays unavailable. Then, handle the remaining standbys: they will still be configured to replicate from the old primary and will stop receiving WAL. Common options are to rebuild them with a fresh base backup from the new primary or attempt pg_rewind if timelines permit. Lastly, treat the old primary as a node to be re-integrated later; do not allow it to come back online accepting writes. This structured flow keeps recovery fast and safe. What step would you automate first in your environment?

Choosing the correct standby hinges on understanding WAL positions. Two standard standby-side functions are pg_last_wal_receive_lsn, which reports the last WAL byte the standby has received from the primary, and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn, which shows the last WAL byte the standby has actually replayed into its data files. For failover safety, prioritize the highest replay_lsn because it reflects applied data. A common pitfall is to compare receive_lsn only: a standby may have received WAL but not yet replayed it, which still risks losing un-applied transactions after promotion. In practice you connect to each standby and run the S Q L checks provided in the chapter. After promotion, confirm the new primary is not in recovery. Also inspect pg_stat_replication on the new primary to learn the state of other standbys. Remember that time and network delays can create small differences; plan for a tolerance window and prefer synchronous standbys where zero-loss is required. Now we'll show exact commands you can copy into a lab environment for verification and practice. Inspecting LSN: pg_last_wal_receive_lsn and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn means compare replay_lsn across standbys and prefer the one with the highest applied wal to minimize data loss on promotion.. In practical terms, how to determine which standby is the freshest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Promotion turns recovery into a writable primary. The recommended approach is pg_ctl promote, which cleanly stops recovery and transitions the server to primary mode. Use the data directory path for the standby. Alternatives can include creating a configured trigger file or removing standby. signal when you fully understand recovery configuration; these methods are less explicit and can be accidental. After promotion, verify the server is no longer in recovery and that you can create a table or run a write statement. A failure to check will hide a non-promoted standby and lead to confusion. Logs will show messages when promotion succeeds; watch them. A common misconception is that promotion immediately restores client access; promotion only changes the server role — you must also update application connection targets. When multiple standbys exist, ensure they are re-pointed to the new primary or rebuilt. The commands below replicate the chapter's safe sequence and are appropriate for lab practice with care. Promoting a Standby: pg_ctl promote and alternatives means use pg_ctl promote for safe, explicit promotion; trigger files and standby.signal removal are alternatives that require precise configuration knowledge.. In practical terms, safe promotion commands and notes about trigger files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After promoting a standby, your database cluster has a new address or role. The absolute critical next step is updating your application's connection string, DNS, or load balancer so client traffic reaches the new primary. Neglecting this leaves applications pointing at the failed host, producing downtime even though the database is now writable. Common mechanisms include updating DNS entry TTLs, changing a load balancer target, or altering application configuration. Each method has tradeoffs: DNS propagation delays can extend downtime unless TTLs were pre-configured low; load balancer updates are faster but require orchestration. A frequent mistake is to rely on automatic client retries without changing endpoints — clients retrying the down host do not magically discover the new primary. When testing, simulate connection switch by updating a single service to the new host and confirm transactions succeed. Also ensure health checks and monitoring pick up the new primary and that automated failover orchestrators, if used, are aware of the new topology. In short, promotion gives you a writable server; updating connections makes it useful. Updating Application Connections means promotion is incomplete until clients can reach the new primary; update dns, load balancers, or application configs immediately to restore service.. In practical terms, why this is the single most critical post-promotion step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. After promoting one standby, other replicas are left pointing at the old primary and will stop receiving WAL. You have two primary courses of action. This chapter lists several common pitfalls that teams repeatedly encounter. The most dangerous is split-brain: if the old primary unexpectedly comes back online and accepts writes while a standby has been promoted, you'll have two divergent transaction histories that can cause irreparable corruption. Prevent this by fencing the old host — keep it off the network or shut it down until re-integration. Promoting an outdated standby is another error: always check replay_lsn. Failing to update application connections is operationally fatal; the database may be restored but applications still point to the failed host. Misuse of pg_rewind is a subtler hazard: pg_rewind can reconcile histories only when timelines are compatible. For heavily diverged timelines, pg_rewind will not work and you must rebuild with a base backup. Let's close by restating the most important concepts. First, failover is an emergency promotion and may risk data loss if standbys lag. Second, switchover is a planned role swap that can achieve zero data loss when you stop writes and wait for standbys to catch up. Third, pg_ctl promote is the recommended command to turn a standby into a primary; alternatives like trigger files require precise configuration. Fourth, split-brain happens when two servers accept writes simultaneously and must be prevented by fencing the old primary. Fifth, check pg_last_wal_replay_lsn when choosing a standby — that value shows applied WAL and is the safest signal. Sixth, pg_rewind can re-sync a recovered primary when timelines are compatible, but default to a fresh pg_basebackup if unsure.
